items.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 7197: Wearable Activity Recognition for Swimming Education: Feature Engineering, Sensor Placement, and Machine Learning Evaluation
items.summary: Wearable activity recognition in swimming education differs from competitive-stroke analysis because children's lessons include brief, transitional, and orientation-dependent skills. We evaluated engineered geometric, statistical, and spectral descriptors extracted from wrist and lower-back wearable recordings during natural lessons. The dataset comprised 45 children, with differing sensor availability; 21 activity labels were considered in historical exploratory analyses. A provenance audit identified variable historical F1 conventions and incomplete participant coverage for several activities. Twelve screened binary tasks were therefore evaluated using outer participant-held-out nested leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) validation with inner-fold Decision Tree feature selection. Across 201 outer-fold instances, the Decision Tree achieved pooled macro-F1 scores ranging from 0.422 to 0.839; the strongest result distinguished Backstroke from Jump Entry and Recovery using three-second wrist windows (40 participants, 294 windows). Four additional classifiers were evaluated on the same saved fold-specific selected features and splits: Random Forest reached macro-F1 0.874 on that task. Signal-processing features were selected in all 201 outer folds, including features labeled Welch PSD in 197 folds (98.0%). Coverage auditing documented why the full 21-class task did not meet participant-support criteria; no fully nested reduced multiclass experiment was performed. A small retrospective agreement check of separately labeled student video clips yielded 18/18 agreements ( =1.00) within one recording and is not representative of study-wide reliability. Sampling-rate provenance and historical fixed-range scaling parameters remain limitations. The results support selected context-restricted activity discrimination, not comprehensive 21-class recognition or universal classifier superiority.

items.title: A passive, battery-free flexible metasurface for implantable millimetre-wave radar glucose sensing
items.summary: Continuous glucose monitors (CGM) break the skin barrier and require periodic sensor replacement. We investigated whether a passive, battery-free flexible metasurface, implanted beneath tissue and read by a commercial 60 GHz radar, can track blood glucose levels. The metasurface contained no electronics or reagents. We fitted a conical helix to the in-phase and quadrature radar signals across the frequency sweep and used its mean radius (the spiral radius) as the glucose-dependent feature. We tested glucose concentrations of 25 to 400 mg/dL in saline solution with and without the metasurface, and 196 to 596 mg/dL of total glucose in porcine whole blood beneath ex vivo porcine tissue and in a murine cadaver model with pulsatile blood flow. The metasurface was essential for achieving a monotonic sensor response; in saline, the coefficient of determination ($R^2$) of a logarithmic fit increased from 0.18 without the metasurface to 0.90 with it. In a murine (rat) cadaver model, the signal's spiral radius increased monotonically with glucose concentration despite pulsatile flow ($R^2$ = 0.91), and this monotonic behavior persisted through up to 6 mm of tissue. Although sensitivity decreased at higher glucose levels, each discrete concentration step remained clearly detectable. These results demonstrate that a shallow, passive implant paired with a commercial radar can effectively track blood glucose without requiring onboard electronics or batteries.

items.title: On-device reinforcement learning-based insulin dosing controller for fully automated insulin delivery
items.summary: IntroductionAutomated insulin delivery (AID) systems integrate continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) with algorithm-driven insulin dosing to enable closed-loop glycemic management for people with type 1 diabetes (T1D). Recent advances in wearable glucose sensing and insulin delivery technologies have enabled increasingly compact AID systems; however, deploying advanced AI-based dosing algorithms directly on resource-constrained wearable devices remains technically challenging. Some AID architectures also rely on external devices, such as smartphones or dedicated controllers, introducing additional communication dependencies into the closed-loop operation.MethodsThis study presents an on-device insulin dosing controller based on the soft actor–critic (SAC) algorithm for resource-constrained AID systems. The proposed approach processes CGM data and makes insulin dosing decisions locally, without relying on external computing devices. To enable embedded deployment, a compressed SAC architecture with a lightweight encoder was developed using quantization-aware training and knowledge distillation, together with an online adaptation mechanism for individualized control. The controller was implemented on a resource-constrained microcontroller and evaluated in a hardware-in-the-loop framework using virtual patients from a T1D simulator.ResultsThe proposed controller achieved an average time-in-range of 83% while maintaining real-time on-device execution with millijoule-level energy consumption per control step.DiscussionThese hardware-in-the-loop and in-silico results demonstrate the technical feasibility of real-time reinforcement learning-based insulin dosing and personalization on a resource-constrained embedded platform, while clinical efficacy and safety require further validation.

items.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 7184: MyoProBand: A Modular Multimodal Wearable for Forearm sEMG and Contextual Sensing
items.summary: Wearable sensing technologies have enabled continuous, non-invasive monitoring of physiological signals, accelerating advances in neuromuscular assessment, rehabilitation, and human-machine interaction. Among these technologies, surface electromyography (sEMG) has become a cornerstone for decoding muscle activity. However, the reliability of sEMG remains highly dependent on user-device interaction factors-including skin-electrode impedance, contact pressure, and skin temperature-that introduce signal variability, degrade long-term stability, and limit the generalizability of machine learning models. Despite their importance, these interaction variables are rarely acquired synchronously with sEMG in existing wearable systems, limiting systematic investigation of their influence on signal quality. Here, we present MyoProBand, a compact multimodal forearm wearable that records multichannel sEMG along with skin-electrode impedance, contact pressure, skin temperature, and inertial measurements. By combining neuromuscular, physiological, and mechanical sensing within a synchronized acquisition framework, the platform enables the characterization of the factors governing sEMG reliability during prolonged use. The MyoProBand incorporates custom analog front-end electronics, multimodal sensor conditioning, and embedded signal synchronization while maintaining a lightweight form factor suitable for experimental and translational research. We evaluated the system in healthy participants to assess hardware performance, multimodal signal synchronization, and operational stability during forearm muscle activity. The results show that the sensing modalities can be recorded within the same experimental session while preserving the primary sEMG acquisition and provide initial observations of how interface variables change during use. MyoProBand is intended as a research platform for collecting multimodal datasets that can support later studies of sEMG variability and robust myoelect

items.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 7144: A Temporally Causal Two-Layer Framework for Wearable EEG Sleep Staging and Short-Horizon Sleep-Transition Forecasting
items.summary: Reliable online sleep monitoring requires sleep-stage estimates and forecasts based only on information available at the time of prediction. This study developed a temporally causal two-layer framework for wearable electroencephalography (EEG) sleep staging and short-horizon sleep-transition forecasting. Using 128 Bitbrain Open Access Sleep (BOAS) recordings from 100 participants, the first layer (M0) performed five-stage sleep classification with causal signal processing and participant-isolated nested validation. The second layer (M1) used strictly cross-fitted histories of M0 stage probabilities to predict transitions from wake or N1 (W/N1) to N2, N3, or REM sleep (N2+) within 60, 90, or 120 s after each observed 30-s epoch. M1 eligibility was determined from M0-predicted stages during training and evaluation, without requiring polysomnography (PSG) stage labels at inference. M0 achieved 0.830 accuracy and 0.704 macro-F1. Under M0-predicted eligibility, M1 achieved AUROC values of 0.801, 0.791, and 0.786 at 60, 90, and 120 s, respectively; complementary PSG-conditioned evaluation yielded 0.814, 0.803, and 0.801. Prediction was stronger during wakefulness than N1, and the benefits of probability history were specific to the future-sleep task. Future-perturbation tests confirmed unchanged pre-boundary outputs under the tested conditions. A frozen M0 replay on three Muse S Gen2 nights further identified stage-specific limitations in cross-device transfer. These findings establish an auditable framework for temporally causal wearable EEG analysis and demonstrate the potential of short-horizon sleep-transition forecasting while identifying its current generalization boundaries.

items.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 7137: Movement-Based Sleep Estimation Using a Smart Mattress: Adaptation of Cole-Kripke Algorithm and Comparison with a Multimodal Wearable
items.summary: Multimodal consumer wearables such as Garmin smartwatches combine movement with physiological signals to estimate sleep, whereas bed-based sensing largely relies on movement alone. How far movement alone, sensed from the bed, can go in estimating sleep is unclear. We adapted the Cole-Kripke algorithm to the movement signal of a WhizPad, a smart mattress with a 30-zone pressure array, using the original coefficients and one device-specific scale factor. Estimates were compared with those of a Garmin smartwatch, a proprietary comparator rather than a reference standard, across 28 paired nights in four participants. Epoch-level agreement between the two systems was high for sleep (98.08%) but substantially poorer for wake (30.76%; Cohen's = 0.346). Over each system's own sleep period, pooled wake after sleep onset (WASO) was 7.3 min lower for the WhizPad and pooled total sleep time (TST) 37.2 min higher, largely through a longer sleep period. The mattress registers bed entry, which Garmin does not export, allowing an exploratory, device-derived estimate of sleep latency that was not independently validated. These findings are descriptive and exploratory, and agreement does not establish the accuracy of either system as no polysomnography (PSG) reference was used. Physiological sensing in the bed and, ultimately, PSG validation are directions for future work.

items.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 7135: Clinical Utility of Wearable Sensors After Hip and Knee Arthroplasty: A Scoping Review
items.summary: Background: Wearable sensors can measure recovery after hip and knee arthroplasty, but clinical utility depends on whether their information changes care. Methods: This scoping review searched PubMed and Europe PMC (September 2026), OpenAlex (October 2026) and supplementary sources. AI-assisted screening, charting and comparative risk-of-bias assessment were followed by a targeted human approval of additional AI source checks. Results: Of 3084 unique records, 273 reports from 243 studies were included; 624 of 980 reports sought could not be assessed in full. Measurement or monitoring featured in 256 reports, association or prediction in 123, feedback or management in 71, and comparative sensor-supported care in 43 (37 studies). None of the 43 AI-assessed comparative results was rated at low risk of bias. Two human verifiers approved 322 additional AI review rows on 8 October 2026, covering comparative findings, candidate eligibility, bias-domain triage and cohort links. This was an unblinded approval exercise, not independent duplicate screening or a new formal risk-of-bias reassessment. Sixteen recovered candidates remained outside the map pending complete charting and reconciliation. Source checks identified denominator and numerical inconsistencies requiring qualified interpretation. Conclusions: Wearables support measurement of recovery; clinical utility remains specific to the action and care programme evaluated. Activity benefits do not establish patient-important benefit, and access limitations, unresolved source discrepancies and provisional AI-derived assessments constrain causal conclusions.

items.title: Smartwatch-Measured Clinician Perceptions of Emergency Department Crowding and Their Association With Objective Metrics: Prospective Observational Study
items.summary: Background: Emergency department (ED) crowding compromises patient safety and increases clinical workload. Existing crowding metrics capture structural indicators but not how clinicians subjectively experience crowding in real time. Clinician perception may provide a complementary measure. Objective: This study aimed to examine the concurrent and temporal associations between clinicians’ real-time ED perceived crowding (EDPC), captured via a smartwatch-based ecological momentary assessment (EMA) system, and 3 objective crowding metrics: the ED occupancy ratio (EDOR), the National Emergency Department Overcrowding Score (NEDOCS), and the ED Work Index (EDWIN). Methods: We conducted a prospective observational study over a continuous 449-hour period (November 25, 2024, 7 AM to December 13, 2024, 11:59 PM) in a single tertiary ED operating under reduced bed capacity and attending-only staffing due to a national physician shortage. We enrolled 28 clinicians (5 attending physicians and 23 charge nurses; mean age 36.3, SD 5.9 years; 21 female and 7 male) by voluntary nonprobability sampling. Clinicians recorded EDPC hourly during active shifts on a continuous 0-200 scale anchored to the NEDOCS crowding categories, from “Not Busy” to “Dangerously Overcrowded.” All valid ratings within each hourly period were aggregated into a single median EDPC value. Interrater agreement was assessed with the Gwet weighted agreement coefficient (AC2) at hourly time points with at least 2 ratings. Main analyses used Pearson correlations between hourly median EDPC and median EDOR, NEDOCS, and EDWIN. Linear mixed-effects models additionally accounted for repeated ratings within clinicians and clustering at the same hourly time point. Time-lagged correlations were exploratory. items.title: Mixed Signals: Weight-Space Programming for EEG and ECG
items.summary: Weight-space programming allows language models to read a trained neural network's weights and edit them. This opens the door to training'' by reasoning rather than through gradient descent. Prior work has demonstrated its functionality and promise for game-playing networks and fixing specific failures in language models, even extending to diffusion models. In this work, we present its applicability to models trained on biosignal data, specifically EEG and ECG data. We show that frontier models are not only able to debug specific faults planted in biosignal-based models without being told what these faults are, but are even capable of writing all the weights of a network from scratch, given only the architecture, the task, and a minimal set of training subjects. In particular, in one set of experiments, a language model was able to match standard gradient-descent training using $6\times$ fewer training subjects, through reasoning alone and without any gradient descent step. Networks written by Claude Opus 5.5 also scored higher than classic hand-crafted EEG pipelines (alpha band power, and common spatial patterns with linear discriminant analysis) when built from the same 5 subjects. We also highlight some of the limitations, which include the inability of language models to improve already well-trained classification models, and their incapacity to reliably recognize, from the weights alone, the task a network was trained on. Overall, our results indicate that weight-space programming can be useful for small networks, such as those deployed on edge devices and wearables, but the concept still requires further investigation before it can be used in practice.

items.title: Cardiac autonomic and behavioral signatures of clinically meaningful weight loss: a 12-week wearable study of 31,126 adults
items.summary: Achieving ≥5% body weight loss is clinically meaningful for reducing cardiometabolic risk, yet most evidence on the physiological and behavioral correlates of early weight loss comes from small, supervised interventions. Whether these adaptations replicate using consumer wearable data in free-living adults is unclear. We analyzed 12 weeks of near-continuous wearable data from 31,126 adults (37.4 ± 10.4 years, 79% male, BMI 29.7 ± 4.2 kg/m2) who initiated a weight-loss goal within a consumer health platform (WHOOP). Participants achieving ≥5% weight loss (n = 4,465; 14.3%) were 1:1 propensity-matched to participants who did not (3,912 pairs; N = 7,824). We compared trajectories of cardiac autonomic function (heart rate variability [HRV], resting heart rate [RHR]), physical activity (Strain), sleep, application engagement, and artificial intelligence (AI) Coach interactions. The weight loss group lost 7.5% of body weight versus 0.9% in the matched group, with greater improvements in HRV (+2.78 ms, 95% CI [1.71, 3.85]) and RHR (−1.75 bpm [−2.10, −1.40]) by Week 12, with between-group differences emerging at Week 4. Physical activity was the strongest behavioral predictor of clinically meaningful weight loss (β = −0.72 [−0.77, −0.67]; OR = 1.22 per Strain unit, 95% CI [1.19, 1.24]). Application engagement and AI Coach interactions, particularly motivation and exercise discussions, were independently associated with ≥5% weight loss and percent weight change. Consumer wearables can capture physiological and behavioral signatures of clinically meaningful early weight loss in free-living adults.

items.title: SynForge-Cardio: a unified multimodal synthetic dataset generation framework for privacy-preserving cardiovascular AI
items.summary: Multimodal cardiovascular AI systems benefit from jointly available chest radiographs, 12-lead electrocardiograms (ECGs), and structured electronic health record (EHR) variables. In practice, multi-institutional model development is constrained by privacy regulations, institutional data silos, and class imbalance for less common findings. Existing open-source synthetic data tools are largely modality-specific: tabular libraries such as Synthetic Data Vault (SDV)/Conditional Tabular Generative Adversarial Network (CTGAN), image generators based on latent diffusion, and time-series methods such as Time-series Generative Adversarial Network (TimeGAN) each require its own setup, configuration, and validation. This study presents SynForge-Cardio, a multimodality orchestration framework for prompt-driven synthetic dataset generation across chest X-ray (CXR), 12-lead ECG, and EHR modalities. items.title: Integrating Deep PPG Representations and Digital Biomarkers for Aortic Stenosis Detection with Peri-TAVI Assessment
items.summary: Access to echocardiography is often limited, delaying recognition of progressive aortic stenosis (AS). A brief, low-cost physiological measurement obtained during routine care could help identify patients who may warrant earlier imaging. Here, we present PulseAS, integrating deep photoplethysmography (PPG) representations, waveform biomarkers and clinical information for high-grade AS screening. Three complementary analyses assessed (1) validation and transfer across cohorts differing in geography and ethnic composition, (2) score-based enrichment of AS and pre-transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) cases, and (3) preoperative and postoperative pulse changes. Using 15-s recordings, separate patient-level cross-validation in EDU (n = 1,209) and MIMIC-III (n = 2,970) yielded AUROCs of 0.818 (PulseAS-XGB) and 0.838 (PulseAS-L2), respectively. In external validation from MIMIC-III to EDU, PulseAS-XGB achieved an AUROC of 0.716, improving to 0.813 after local adaptation. The highest-scoring 10% captured 45.2% of all high-grade AS cases in EDU and 41.3% in MIMIC-III, and 56.9% of pre-TAVI cases in EDU. Notably, in the EDU TAVI subgroup, PPG waveforms showed earlier systolic peaks and narrower systolic contours following intervention. These findings support clinical-PPG risk stratification in new populations and warrant prospective evaluation of echocardiographic prioritisation.

items.title: A Synchronized Tri-Modality Wireless System for Multi-Point Non-Contact Cardiac Monitoring
items.summary: Cardiac physiological monitoring is fundamental to evaluating cardiovascular health and diagnosing related diseases. Non-contact radar sensing can capture chest-wall vibrations with spatial specificity, enabling localized physiological monitoring and cardiac assessment. Progress, however, has been limited by the absence of a reliable, research-grade hardware platform for rigorous validation of radar-based methods. Prior systems typically pair radar, namely Doppler cardiography (DCG), with only electrocardiography (ECG) or other coarse references, providing no direct mechanical ground truth and thus constraining fine-grained evaluation of radar outputs. We present a tri-modality wireless system that integrates ECG, seismocardiography (SCG), and DCG under a unified acquisition and control framework for time-aligned recording and analysis. The tri-modality system combines miniaturized wearable ECG/SCG modules with a high-resolution mmWave radar module, supporting spatially resolved sensing and subsequent feature extraction. To our knowledge, this is the first integrated ECG--SCG--DCG hardware system for comprehensive cardiac monitoring; it enables multi-point thoracic acquisition, achieves precise cross-modal synchronization, and maintains specifications suitable for wearable operation. Experiments on a linear-motion platform show close agreement between DCG- and SCG-derived displacements, confirming accurate displacement measurement. Human-subject studies further demonstrate cross-modal consistency and robust extraction of feature points, establishing ECG as the electrical anchor and SCG as the mechanical ground truth for DCG. Overall, the system provides a rigorous, spatially resolved validation platform that advances non-contact cardiac sensing and supports next-generation radar-based monitoring.

items.title: Slide to Report: Continuous Reporting Symptom-Specific Cybersickness in VR
items.summary: Cybersickness is often assessed during VR exposure through discrete overall sickness, which cannot capture specific symptoms or their changes over time. Post-exposure questionnaires such as the Simulator Sickness Questionnaire provide symptom-specific measures but cannot be collected during immersion. We investigate whether separating cybersickness into three symptom-specific dimensions -- nausea, oculomotor discomfort, and disorientation -- during immersion provides more informative continuous measurements. We conducted a between-subjects study with 52 participants in a VR-rollercoaster, comparing a three-slider interface with a single-slider interface. Concurrently, participants also completed an auditory Simon task to measure attention. We additionally collected multimodal set of physiological signals, including GSR, ECG, PPG, eye and head tracking. Results show that each slider correlated most strongly with its corresponding SSQ subscale, whereas the single slider correlated with all SSQ subscales. Using three sliders did not significantly affect usability, workload, or attention. We publicly release the multimodal dataset to support future cybersickness research.

items.title: MultiMental-IAS: A Multimodal Driver Mental State Analysis Dataset for Context-Aware Non-IID Evaluation
items.summary: Robust driver-state modelling requires synchronized physiological, behavioural, and contextual signals, yet existing open resources typically target a single cognitive state, omit continuous vehicle context, or do not define evaluation protocols that expose inter-subject heterogeneity. We present Multimental-IAS, a multimodal driver mental-state dataset collected in a cockpit-in-the-loop simulation built on CARLA. It contains vehicle telemetry with scenario-context channels, four-channel EEG and three-channel PPG from a Muse 2 headband, and cabin-facing video from 23 participants, recorded in 148 trials (11.6 hours) under six induced states: Normal, Distracted, Alerted, Stressed, Relaxed, and Drowsy. We document the acquisition pipeline in detail and provide a benchmark with one protocol for all models: chronological within-subject splits, participant-disjoint cross-subject folds, validation-based model selection, and ablations over modalities, scenario-context channels, and signal normalization. Multimodal fusion reaches a macro-F1 of 0.94 for drivers seen during training. For unseen drivers, fusing driving dynamics with per-window normalized EEG/PPG raises macro-F1 from 0.408 (telemetry alone) to 0.485, consistently across all five folds, while the gap between the two protocols quantifies the inter-driver heterogeneity that personalized models must address. Multimental-IAS thus provides a concrete testbed for non-IID generalization, personalization, and federated learning in driver monitoring.

items.title: Evaluating Generalization and Long-Term Stability of Smartwatch-Based Cuffless Blood Pressure Monitoring
items.summary: Smartwatch-based cuffless blood pressure (BP) monitoring is a promising low-burden solution for long-term cardiovascular management, but practical deployment remains constrained by model complexity, uncertain cross-dataset generalization, and insufficient evidence on long-term tracking stability. This study presents an efficient Signal-Context Gated Fusion Network (SCGBPNet) for cuffless BP estimation from photoplethysmography (PPG) signals. SCGBPNet integrates signal-level representations through self-attention and further incorporates subject-specific contextual information via a compact gated fusion module. On Aurora-BP, SCGBPNet achieved SBP/DBP mean absolute errors (MAEs) of 7.08/4.90 mmHg, compared with 6.44/4.89 mmHg under within-dataset validation on the private smartwatch dataset, indicating a modest within-dataset discrepancy. Cross-dataset transfer from Aurora-BP to the smartwatch dataset increased the MAEs to 8.98/6.47 mmHg, demonstrating substantial cross-dataset degradation. For long-term stability, the proposed method showed low week-to-week performance variation and a low daily decay rate, indicating good stability over a follow-up period of more than one month. Nevertheless, estimation accuracy deteriorated when BP deviated substantially from an individual's baseline. These findings indicate that favorable aggregate MAE alone should not be interpreted as evidence of deployment-ready performance. More systematic and stratified evaluation across dataset settings, BP ranges, and baseline-deviation levels is needed to assess the practical reliability of smartwatch-based cuffless BP monitoring.

items.title: Robust PPG-Exclusive Heart Rate Estimation During Maximal Exercise Using Population-Based Priors
items.summary: PPG is the main technology for wearable heart rate (HR) monitoring. However, motion artifacts during intense physical activity reduce its reliability due to spectral overlap with the cardiac signal. This study investigates whether severely contaminated PPG signals can yield reliable HR estimates without auxiliary sensors by leveraging prior knowledge of HR dynamics. We acquired simultaneous PPG and ECG signals from 21 subjects during a maximal cycloergometer test. Using Leave-One-Subject-Out cross-validation, we built HR evolution priors from the ground-truth ECG and applied Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) to align normalized HR curves and estimate a barycenter average. DTW aligns normalized HR curves with minimal error across all subjects, validating robust population-based priors. For each test subject, we combined the PPG Power Spectral Density (PSD) with the prior distribution to generate a "posterior PSD". We identified and ranked candidate HR trajectories using heuristic search within the "posterior PSD" and selected the most likely path. Our approach reduced mean absolute error (MAE) in BPM relative to the ground-truth ECG by a median of 63.3% (IQR: 47.3%-74.6%) compared to a PPG+accelerometer benchmark. These results show that physiological priors and DTW-based alignment enable robust, PPG-exclusive HR monitoring during high-intensity exercise.

items.title: MM-Net: A Multimodal Multi-Task Network for Sleep Staging and Sleep Apnea Assessment After Ischemic Stroke
items.summary: Automated polysomnography after ischemic stroke is challenging because of altered sleep-related neural activity and concurrent respiratory disturbances. Existing stroke-specific approaches mainly address sleep-stage classification, leaving joint analysis of sleep architecture and respiratory events underexplored. Moreover, adapting pretrained EEG encoders introduces a representation inconsistency when downstream models are trained on embeddings from previously seen patients but evaluated on unseen individuals. We propose MM-Net, a multimodal multi-task framework that resolves this inconsistency through cross-fitting and ridge-based embedding alignment. Sleep-adapted EEG-EOG representations and engineered neural descriptors are fused with learned cardiorespiratory features through cross-attention and shared temporal modeling for simultaneous sleep staging and respiratory-event detection. On iSLEEPS (99 patients with subacute ischemic stroke), ten-fold patient-independent evaluation achieved 76.3% staging accuracy (Cohen's $κ$ = 0.656) and 0.825 respiratory-event AUC, outperforming the evaluated baselines under matched protocols. The sleep-adapted encoder improved the downstream model when its embeddings were aligned, raising staging accuracy by 1.4 percentage points over the frozen encoder ($p$ = 0.020) versus 0.2 points without alignment. MM-Net also achieved 86.4% staging accuracy on Sleep-EDF, above every single-EEG architecture reimplemented on the same recordings, and 80.3% staging accuracy with 0.889 respiratory AUC on ISRUC-I, exceeding its retrained staging baselines. Without retraining, the iSLEEPS-trained model retained respiratory AUCs of 0.833 on ISRUC-I and 0.841 on UCD. These findings support representation-consistent neural adaptation and joint physiological modeling across stroke, healthy-sleep, and sleep-disorder cohorts.

items.title: The Metrology Atlas: describing recorded physiological data as a measurement system, with VitalDB as a first application
items.summary: Every value in a recorded physiological dataset is a pair: a recorded time and a recorded value. Neither is the truth. The time comes from a clock that drifts and is corrected in jumps, and often describes a window that ended earlier. The value was quantised, rounded, sometimes heaped by hand, and measured by an instrument with its own error. We present the Metrology Atlas, a dataset-independent way of describing a recorded dataset as a measurement system, and its first application, to VitalDB, an open dataset of 6,388 surgical patients, as a proof of principle. For every variable, the atlas states what was measured, the measurement model linking it to the recorded pair, and what is known about the true time and true value given a record. Each part of the model carries its evidence: 69 studies, 49 parameters and 54 observations, each marked as measured, derived, estimated or assumed. The atlas maps 11 clocks and 14 devices into one timing network, and closes loops in that network to test its own model. Synchronisation reduces the median timing error between the EEG and ECG from 794 ms to 42 ms, and between ventilator and monitor waveforms from 378 ms to 55 ms. The atlas also documents data-quality issues, several of which correct the dataset's own documentation. It is published as a website and a single machine-readable file, with open-source code and a scheme of time-aware labels. Everything is open under CC BY 4.0 and MIT licences. The engine, schema and timing tools carry over unchanged, and the aim is to describe many other datasets the same way.

academic.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 7197: Wearable Activity Recognition for Swimming Education: Feature Engineering, Sensor Placement, and Machine Learning Evaluation
academic.summary: Wearable activity recognition in swimming education differs from competitive-stroke analysis because children's lessons include brief, transitional, and orientation-dependent skills. We evaluated engineered geometric, statistical, and spectral descriptors extracted from wrist and lower-back wearable recordings during natural lessons. The dataset comprised 45 children, with differing sensor availability; 21 activity labels were considered in historical exploratory analyses. A provenance audit identified variable historical F1 conventions and incomplete participant coverage for several activities. Twelve screened binary tasks were therefore evaluated using outer participant-held-out nested leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) validation with inner-fold Decision Tree feature selection. Across 201 outer-fold instances, the Decision Tree achieved pooled macro-F1 scores ranging from 0.422 to 0.839; the strongest result distinguished Backstroke from Jump Entry and Recovery using three-second wrist windows (40 participants, 294 windows). Four additional classifiers were evaluated on the same saved fold-specific selected features and splits: Random Forest reached macro-F1 0.874 on that task. Signal-processing features were selected in all 201 outer folds, including features labeled Welch PSD in 197 folds (98.0%). Coverage auditing documented why the full 21-class task did not meet participant-support criteria; no fully nested reduced multiclass experiment was performed. A small retrospective agreement check of separately labeled student video clips yielded 18/18 agreements ( =1.00) within one recording and is not representative of study-wide reliability. Sampling-rate provenance and historical fixed-range scaling parameters remain limitations. The results support selected context-restricted activity discrimination, not comprehensive 21-class recognition or universal classifier superiority.

academic.title: A passive, battery-free flexible metasurface for implantable millimetre-wave radar glucose sensing
academic.summary: Continuous glucose monitors (CGM) break the skin barrier and require periodic sensor replacement. We investigated whether a passive, battery-free flexible metasurface, implanted beneath tissue and read by a commercial 60 GHz radar, can track blood glucose levels. The metasurface contained no electronics or reagents. We fitted a conical helix to the in-phase and quadrature radar signals across the frequency sweep and used its mean radius (the spiral radius) as the glucose-dependent feature. We tested glucose concentrations of 25 to 400 mg/dL in saline solution with and without the metasurface, and 196 to 596 mg/dL of total glucose in porcine whole blood beneath ex vivo porcine tissue and in a murine cadaver model with pulsatile blood flow. The metasurface was essential for achieving a monotonic sensor response; in saline, the coefficient of determination ($R^2$) of a logarithmic fit increased from 0.18 without the metasurface to 0.90 with it. In a murine (rat) cadaver model, the signal's spiral radius increased monotonically with glucose concentration despite pulsatile flow ($R^2$ = 0.91), and this monotonic behavior persisted through up to 6 mm of tissue. Although sensitivity decreased at higher glucose levels, each discrete concentration step remained clearly detectable. These results demonstrate that a shallow, passive implant paired with a commercial radar can effectively track blood glucose without requiring onboard electronics or batteries.

academic.title: On-device reinforcement learning-based insulin dosing controller for fully automated insulin delivery
academic.summary: IntroductionAutomated insulin delivery (AID) systems integrate continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) with algorithm-driven insulin dosing to enable closed-loop glycemic management for people with type 1 diabetes (T1D). Recent advances in wearable glucose sensing and insulin delivery technologies have enabled increasingly compact AID systems; however, deploying advanced AI-based dosing algorithms directly on resource-constrained wearable devices remains technically challenging. Some AID architectures also rely on external devices, such as smartphones or dedicated controllers, introducing additional communication dependencies into the closed-loop operation.MethodsThis study presents an on-device insulin dosing controller based on the soft actor–critic (SAC) algorithm for resource-constrained AID systems. The proposed approach processes CGM data and makes insulin dosing decisions locally, without relying on external computing devices. To enable embedded deployment, a compressed SAC architecture with a lightweight encoder was developed using quantization-aware training and knowledge distillation, together with an online adaptation mechanism for individualized control. The controller was implemented on a resource-constrained microcontroller and evaluated in a hardware-in-the-loop framework using virtual patients from a T1D simulator.ResultsThe proposed controller achieved an average time-in-range of 83% while maintaining real-time on-device execution with millijoule-level energy consumption per control step.DiscussionThese hardware-in-the-loop and in-silico results demonstrate the technical feasibility of real-time reinforcement learning-based insulin dosing and personalization on a resource-constrained embedded platform, while clinical efficacy and safety require further validation.

academic.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 7184: MyoProBand: A Modular Multimodal Wearable for Forearm sEMG and Contextual Sensing
academic.summary: Wearable sensing technologies have enabled continuous, non-invasive monitoring of physiological signals, accelerating advances in neuromuscular assessment, rehabilitation, and human-machine interaction. Among these technologies, surface electromyography (sEMG) has become a cornerstone for decoding muscle activity. However, the reliability of sEMG remains highly dependent on user-device interaction factors-including skin-electrode impedance, contact pressure, and skin temperature-that introduce signal variability, degrade long-term stability, and limit the generalizability of machine learning models. Despite their importance, these interaction variables are rarely acquired synchronously with sEMG in existing wearable systems, limiting systematic investigation of their influence on signal quality. Here, we present MyoProBand, a compact multimodal forearm wearable that records multichannel sEMG along with skin-electrode impedance, contact pressure, skin temperature, and inertial measurements. By combining neuromuscular, physiological, and mechanical sensing within a synchronized acquisition framework, the platform enables the characterization of the factors governing sEMG reliability during prolonged use. The MyoProBand incorporates custom analog front-end electronics, multimodal sensor conditioning, and embedded signal synchronization while maintaining a lightweight form factor suitable for experimental and translational research. We evaluated the system in healthy participants to assess hardware performance, multimodal signal synchronization, and operational stability during forearm muscle activity. The results show that the sensing modalities can be recorded within the same experimental session while preserving the primary sEMG acquisition and provide initial observations of how interface variables change during use. MyoProBand is intended as a research platform for collecting multimodal datasets that can support later studies of sEMG variability and robust myoelect

academic.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 7144: A Temporally Causal Two-Layer Framework for Wearable EEG Sleep Staging and Short-Horizon Sleep-Transition Forecasting
academic.summary: Reliable online sleep monitoring requires sleep-stage estimates and forecasts based only on information available at the time of prediction. This study developed a temporally causal two-layer framework for wearable electroencephalography (EEG) sleep staging and short-horizon sleep-transition forecasting. Using 128 Bitbrain Open Access Sleep (BOAS) recordings from 100 participants, the first layer (M0) performed five-stage sleep classification with causal signal processing and participant-isolated nested validation. The second layer (M1) used strictly cross-fitted histories of M0 stage probabilities to predict transitions from wake or N1 (W/N1) to N2, N3, or REM sleep (N2+) within 60, 90, or 120 s after each observed 30-s epoch. M1 eligibility was determined from M0-predicted stages during training and evaluation, without requiring polysomnography (PSG) stage labels at inference. M0 achieved 0.830 accuracy and 0.704 macro-F1. Under M0-predicted eligibility, M1 achieved AUROC values of 0.801, 0.791, and 0.786 at 60, 90, and 120 s, respectively; complementary PSG-conditioned evaluation yielded 0.814, 0.803, and 0.801. Prediction was stronger during wakefulness than N1, and the benefits of probability history were specific to the future-sleep task. Future-perturbation tests confirmed unchanged pre-boundary outputs under the tested conditions. A frozen M0 replay on three Muse S Gen2 nights further identified stage-specific limitations in cross-device transfer. These findings establish an auditable framework for temporally causal wearable EEG analysis and demonstrate the potential of short-horizon sleep-transition forecasting while identifying its current generalization boundaries.

academic.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 7137: Movement-Based Sleep Estimation Using a Smart Mattress: Adaptation of Cole-Kripke Algorithm and Comparison with a Multimodal Wearable
academic.summary: Multimodal consumer wearables such as Garmin smartwatches combine movement with physiological signals to estimate sleep, whereas bed-based sensing largely relies on movement alone. How far movement alone, sensed from the bed, can go in estimating sleep is unclear. We adapted the Cole-Kripke algorithm to the movement signal of a WhizPad, a smart mattress with a 30-zone pressure array, using the original coefficients and one device-specific scale factor. Estimates were compared with those of a Garmin smartwatch, a proprietary comparator rather than a reference standard, across 28 paired nights in four participants. Epoch-level agreement between the two systems was high for sleep (98.08%) but substantially poorer for wake (30.76%; Cohen's = 0.346). Over each system's own sleep period, pooled wake after sleep onset (WASO) was 7.3 min lower for the WhizPad and pooled total sleep time (TST) 37.2 min higher, largely through a longer sleep period. The mattress registers bed entry, which Garmin does not export, allowing an exploratory, device-derived estimate of sleep latency that was not independently validated. These findings are descriptive and exploratory, and agreement does not establish the accuracy of either system as no polysomnography (PSG) reference was used. Physiological sensing in the bed and, ultimately, PSG validation are directions for future work.

academic.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 7135: Clinical Utility of Wearable Sensors After Hip and Knee Arthroplasty: A Scoping Review
academic.summary: Background: Wearable sensors can measure recovery after hip and knee arthroplasty, but clinical utility depends on whether their information changes care. Methods: This scoping review searched PubMed and Europe PMC (September 2026), OpenAlex (October 2026) and supplementary sources. AI-assisted screening, charting and comparative risk-of-bias assessment were followed by a targeted human approval of additional AI source checks. Results: Of 3084 unique records, 273 reports from 243 studies were included; 624 of 980 reports sought could not be assessed in full. Measurement or monitoring featured in 256 reports, association or prediction in 123, feedback or management in 71, and comparative sensor-supported care in 43 (37 studies). None of the 43 AI-assessed comparative results was rated at low risk of bias. Two human verifiers approved 322 additional AI review rows on 8 October 2026, covering comparative findings, candidate eligibility, bias-domain triage and cohort links. This was an unblinded approval exercise, not independent duplicate screening or a new formal risk-of-bias reassessment. Sixteen recovered candidates remained outside the map pending complete charting and reconciliation. Source checks identified denominator and numerical inconsistencies requiring qualified interpretation. Conclusions: Wearables support measurement of recovery; clinical utility remains specific to the action and care programme evaluated. Activity benefits do not establish patient-important benefit, and access limitations, unresolved source discrepancies and provisional AI-derived assessments constrain causal conclusions.

academic.title: Smartwatch-Measured Clinician Perceptions of Emergency Department Crowding and Their Association With Objective Metrics: Prospective Observational Study
academic.summary: Background: Emergency department (ED) crowding compromises patient safety and increases clinical workload. Existing crowding metrics capture structural indicators but not how clinicians subjectively experience crowding in real time. Clinician perception may provide a complementary measure. Methods: We conducted a prospective observational study over a continuous 449-hour period (November 25, 2024, 7 AM to December 13, 2024, 11:59 PM) in a single tertiary ED operating under reduced bed capacity and attending-only staffing due to a national physician shortage. We enrolled 28 clinicians (5 attending physicians and 23 charge nurses; mean age 36.3, SD 5.9 years; 21 female and 7 male) by voluntary nonprobability sampling. Clinicians recorded EDPC hourly during active shifts on a continuous 0-200 scale anchored to the NEDOCS crowding categories, from “Not Busy” to “Dangerously Overcrowded.” All valid ratings within each hourly period were aggregated into a single median EDPC value. Interrater agreement was assessed with the Gwet weighted agreement coefficient (AC2) at hourly time points with at least 2 ratings. Main analyses used Pearson correlations between hourly median EDPC and median EDOR, NEDOCS, and EDWIN. Linear mixed-effects models additionally accounted for repeated ratings within clinicians and clustering at the same hourly time point. Time-lagged correlations were exploratory. Statistical significance was set at α=.05. Results: Across 1124 scheduled on-duty assessment opportunities, clinicians completed 1100 individual EDPC ratings (response rate 1100/1124, 97.86%). academic.title: Mixed Signals: Weight-Space Programming for EEG and ECG
academic.summary: Weight-space programming allows language models to read a trained neural network's weights and edit them. This opens the door to training'' by reasoning rather than through gradient descent. Prior work has demonstrated its functionality and promise for game-playing networks and fixing specific failures in language models, even extending to diffusion models. In this work, we present its applicability to models trained on biosignal data, specifically EEG and ECG data. We show that frontier models are not only able to debug specific faults planted in biosignal-based models without being told what these faults are, but are even capable of writing all the weights of a network from scratch, given only the architecture, the task, and a minimal set of training subjects. In particular, in one set of experiments, a language model was able to match standard gradient-descent training using $6\times$ fewer training subjects, through reasoning alone and without any gradient descent step. Networks written by Claude Opus 5.5 also scored higher than classic hand-crafted EEG pipelines (alpha band power, and common spatial patterns with linear discriminant analysis) when built from the same 5 subjects. We also highlight some of the limitations, which include the inability of language models to improve already well-trained classification models, and their incapacity to reliably recognize, from the weights alone, the task a network was trained on. Overall, our results indicate that weight-space programming can be useful for small networks, such as those deployed on edge devices and wearables, but the concept still requires further investigation before it can be used in practice.

academic.title: Cardiac autonomic and behavioral signatures of clinically meaningful weight loss: a 12-week wearable study of 31,126 adults
academic.summary: Achieving ≥5% body weight loss is clinically meaningful for reducing cardiometabolic risk, yet most evidence on the physiological and behavioral correlates of early weight loss comes from small, supervised interventions. Whether these adaptations replicate using consumer wearable data in free-living adults is unclear. We analyzed 12 weeks of near-continuous wearable data from 31,126 adults (37.4 ± 10.4 years, 79% male, BMI 29.7 ± 4.2 kg/m2) who initiated a weight-loss goal within a consumer health platform (WHOOP). Participants achieving ≥5% weight loss (n = 4,465; 14.3%) were 1:1 propensity-matched to participants who did not (3,912 pairs; N = 7,824). We compared trajectories of cardiac autonomic function (heart rate variability [HRV], resting heart rate [RHR]), physical activity (Strain), sleep, application engagement, and artificial intelligence (AI) Coach interactions. The weight loss group lost 7.5% of body weight versus 0.9% in the matched group, with greater improvements in HRV (+2.78 ms, 95% CI [1.71, 3.85]) and RHR (−1.75 bpm [−2.10, −1.40]) by Week 12, with between-group differences emerging at Week 4. Physical activity was the strongest behavioral predictor of clinically meaningful weight loss (β = −0.72 [−0.77, −0.67]; OR = 1.22 per Strain unit, 95% CI [1.19, 1.24]). Application engagement and AI Coach interactions, particularly motivation and exercise discussions, were independently associated with ≥5% weight loss and percent weight change. Consumer wearables can capture physiological and behavioral signatures of clinically meaningful early weight loss in free-living adults.

academic.title: SynForge-Cardio: a unified multimodal synthetic dataset generation framework for privacy-preserving cardiovascular AI
academic.summary: Multimodal cardiovascular AI systems benefit from jointly available chest radiographs, 12-lead electrocardiograms (ECGs), and structured electronic health record (EHR) variables. In practice, multi-institutional model development is constrained by privacy regulations, institutional data silos, and class imbalance for less common findings. Existing open-source synthetic data tools are largely modality-specific: tabular libraries such as Synthetic Data Vault (SDV)/Conditional Tabular Generative Adversarial Network (CTGAN), image generators based on latent diffusion, and time-series methods such as Time-series Generative Adversarial Network (TimeGAN) each require its own setup, configuration, and validation. This study presents SynForge-Cardio, a multimodality orchestration framework for prompt-driven synthetic dataset generation across chest X-ray (CXR), 12-lead ECG, and EHR modalities. Rather than introducing a new generative backbone, SynForge-Cardio coordinates established components—latent diffusion with optional low-rank adaptation for CXR; parametric and bounded morphology-preserving augmentation (with an optional TimeGAN path) for ECG; and size-aware routing among jitter augmentation, Gaussian copula, and CTGAN/Tabular Variational Autoencoder for EHR—behind a shared clinical prompt interface, a rule-based router, and a postgeneration quality/privacy reporting layer. The three modalities were generated independently from separate datasets; the framework does not perform patient-level joint synthesis and makes no claim of anatomical or physiological consistency across modalities. academic.title: Integrating Deep PPG Representations and Digital Biomarkers for Aortic Stenosis Detection with Peri-TAVI Assessment
academic.summary: Access to echocardiography is often limited, delaying recognition of progressive aortic stenosis (AS). A brief, low-cost physiological measurement obtained during routine care could help identify patients who may warrant earlier imaging. Here, we present PulseAS, integrating deep photoplethysmography (PPG) representations, waveform biomarkers and clinical information for high-grade AS screening. Three complementary analyses assessed (1) validation and transfer across cohorts differing in geography and ethnic composition, (2) score-based enrichment of AS and pre-transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) cases, and (3) preoperative and postoperative pulse changes. Using 15-s recordings, separate patient-level cross-validation in EDU (n = 1,209) and MIMIC-III (n = 2,970) yielded AUROCs of 0.818 (PulseAS-XGB) and 0.838 (PulseAS-L2), respectively. In external validation from MIMIC-III to EDU, PulseAS-XGB achieved an AUROC of 0.716, improving to 0.813 after local adaptation. The highest-scoring 10% captured 45.2% of all high-grade AS cases in EDU and 41.3% in MIMIC-III, and 56.9% of pre-TAVI cases in EDU. Notably, in the EDU TAVI subgroup, PPG waveforms showed earlier systolic peaks and narrower systolic contours following intervention. These findings support clinical-PPG risk stratification in new populations and warrant prospective evaluation of echocardiographic prioritisation.

academic.title: A Synchronized Tri-Modality Wireless System for Multi-Point Non-Contact Cardiac Monitoring
academic.summary: Cardiac physiological monitoring is fundamental to evaluating cardiovascular health and diagnosing related diseases. Non-contact radar sensing can capture chest-wall vibrations with spatial specificity, enabling localized physiological monitoring and cardiac assessment. Progress, however, has been limited by the absence of a reliable, research-grade hardware platform for rigorous validation of radar-based methods. Prior systems typically pair radar, namely Doppler cardiography (DCG), with only electrocardiography (ECG) or other coarse references, providing no direct mechanical ground truth and thus constraining fine-grained evaluation of radar outputs. We present a tri-modality wireless system that integrates ECG, seismocardiography (SCG), and DCG under a unified acquisition and control framework for time-aligned recording and analysis. The tri-modality system combines miniaturized wearable ECG/SCG modules with a high-resolution mmWave radar module, supporting spatially resolved sensing and subsequent feature extraction. To our knowledge, this is the first integrated ECG--SCG--DCG hardware system for comprehensive cardiac monitoring; it enables multi-point thoracic acquisition, achieves precise cross-modal synchronization, and maintains specifications suitable for wearable operation. Experiments on a linear-motion platform show close agreement between DCG- and SCG-derived displacements, confirming accurate displacement measurement. Human-subject studies further demonstrate cross-modal consistency and robust extraction of feature points, establishing ECG as the electrical anchor and SCG as the mechanical ground truth for DCG. Overall, the system provides a rigorous, spatially resolved validation platform that advances non-contact cardiac sensing and supports next-generation radar-based monitoring.

academic.title: Slide to Report: Continuous Reporting Symptom-Specific Cybersickness in VR
academic.summary: Cybersickness is often assessed during VR exposure through discrete overall sickness, which cannot capture specific symptoms or their changes over time. Post-exposure questionnaires such as the Simulator Sickness Questionnaire provide symptom-specific measures but cannot be collected during immersion. We investigate whether separating cybersickness into three symptom-specific dimensions -- nausea, oculomotor discomfort, and disorientation -- during immersion provides more informative continuous measurements. We conducted a between-subjects study with 52 participants in a VR-rollercoaster, comparing a three-slider interface with a single-slider interface. Concurrently, participants also completed an auditory Simon task to measure attention. We additionally collected multimodal set of physiological signals, including GSR, ECG, PPG, eye and head tracking. Results show that each slider correlated most strongly with its corresponding SSQ subscale, whereas the single slider correlated with all SSQ subscales. Using three sliders did not significantly affect usability, workload, or attention. We publicly release the multimodal dataset to support future cybersickness research.

academic.title: MultiMental-IAS: A Multimodal Driver Mental State Analysis Dataset for Context-Aware Non-IID Evaluation
academic.summary: Robust driver-state modelling requires synchronized physiological, behavioural, and contextual signals, yet existing open resources typically target a single cognitive state, omit continuous vehicle context, or do not define evaluation protocols that expose inter-subject heterogeneity. We present Multimental-IAS, a multimodal driver mental-state dataset collected in a cockpit-in-the-loop simulation built on CARLA. It contains vehicle telemetry with scenario-context channels, four-channel EEG and three-channel PPG from a Muse 2 headband, and cabin-facing video from 23 participants, recorded in 148 trials (11.6 hours) under six induced states: Normal, Distracted, Alerted, Stressed, Relaxed, and Drowsy. We document the acquisition pipeline in detail and provide a benchmark with one protocol for all models: chronological within-subject splits, participant-disjoint cross-subject folds, validation-based model selection, and ablations over modalities, scenario-context channels, and signal normalization. Multimodal fusion reaches a macro-F1 of 0.94 for drivers seen during training. For unseen drivers, fusing driving dynamics with per-window normalized EEG/PPG raises macro-F1 from 0.408 (telemetry alone) to 0.485, consistently across all five folds, while the gap between the two protocols quantifies the inter-driver heterogeneity that personalized models must address. Multimental-IAS thus provides a concrete testbed for non-IID generalization, personalization, and federated learning in driver monitoring.

academic.title: Evaluating Generalization and Long-Term Stability of Smartwatch-Based Cuffless Blood Pressure Monitoring
academic.summary: Smartwatch-based cuffless blood pressure (BP) monitoring is a promising low-burden solution for long-term cardiovascular management, but practical deployment remains constrained by model complexity, uncertain cross-dataset generalization, and insufficient evidence on long-term tracking stability. This study presents an efficient Signal-Context Gated Fusion Network (SCGBPNet) for cuffless BP estimation from photoplethysmography (PPG) signals. SCGBPNet integrates signal-level representations through self-attention and further incorporates subject-specific contextual information via a compact gated fusion module. On Aurora-BP, SCGBPNet achieved SBP/DBP mean absolute errors (MAEs) of 7.08/4.90 mmHg, compared with 6.44/4.89 mmHg under within-dataset validation on the private smartwatch dataset, indicating a modest within-dataset discrepancy. Cross-dataset transfer from Aurora-BP to the smartwatch dataset increased the MAEs to 8.98/6.47 mmHg, demonstrating substantial cross-dataset degradation. For long-term stability, the proposed method showed low week-to-week performance variation and a low daily decay rate, indicating good stability over a follow-up period of more than one month. Nevertheless, estimation accuracy deteriorated when BP deviated substantially from an individual's baseline. These findings indicate that favorable aggregate MAE alone should not be interpreted as evidence of deployment-ready performance. More systematic and stratified evaluation across dataset settings, BP ranges, and baseline-deviation levels is needed to assess the practical reliability of smartwatch-based cuffless BP monitoring.

academic.title: Robust PPG-Exclusive Heart Rate Estimation During Maximal Exercise Using Population-Based Priors
academic.summary: PPG is the main technology for wearable heart rate (HR) monitoring. However, motion artifacts during intense physical activity reduce its reliability due to spectral overlap with the cardiac signal. This study investigates whether severely contaminated PPG signals can yield reliable HR estimates without auxiliary sensors by leveraging prior knowledge of HR dynamics. We acquired simultaneous PPG and ECG signals from 21 subjects during a maximal cycloergometer test. Using Leave-One-Subject-Out cross-validation, we built HR evolution priors from the ground-truth ECG and applied Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) to align normalized HR curves and estimate a barycenter average. DTW aligns normalized HR curves with minimal error across all subjects, validating robust population-based priors. For each test subject, we combined the PPG Power Spectral Density (PSD) with the prior distribution to generate a "posterior PSD". We identified and ranked candidate HR trajectories using heuristic search within the "posterior PSD" and selected the most likely path. Our approach reduced mean absolute error (MAE) in BPM relative to the ground-truth ECG by a median of 63.3% (IQR: 47.3%-74.6%) compared to a PPG+accelerometer benchmark. These results show that physiological priors and DTW-based alignment enable robust, PPG-exclusive HR monitoring during high-intensity exercise.

academic.title: MM-Net: A Multimodal Multi-Task Network for Sleep Staging and Sleep Apnea Assessment After Ischemic Stroke
academic.summary: Automated polysomnography after ischemic stroke is challenging because of altered sleep-related neural activity and concurrent respiratory disturbances. Existing stroke-specific approaches mainly address sleep-stage classification, leaving joint analysis of sleep architecture and respiratory events underexplored. Moreover, adapting pretrained EEG encoders introduces a representation inconsistency when downstream models are trained on embeddings from previously seen patients but evaluated on unseen individuals. We propose MM-Net, a multimodal multi-task framework that resolves this inconsistency through cross-fitting and ridge-based embedding alignment. Sleep-adapted EEG-EOG representations and engineered neural descriptors are fused with learned cardiorespiratory features through cross-attention and shared temporal modeling for simultaneous sleep staging and respiratory-event detection. On iSLEEPS (99 patients with subacute ischemic stroke), ten-fold patient-independent evaluation achieved 76.3% staging accuracy (Cohen's $κ$ = 0.656) and 0.825 respiratory-event AUC, outperforming the evaluated baselines under matched protocols. The sleep-adapted encoder improved the downstream model when its embeddings were aligned, raising staging accuracy by 1.4 percentage points over the frozen encoder ($p$ = 0.020) versus 0.2 points without alignment. MM-Net also achieved 86.4% staging accuracy on Sleep-EDF, above every single-EEG architecture reimplemented on the same recordings, and 80.3% staging accuracy with 0.889 respiratory AUC on ISRUC-I, exceeding its retrained staging baselines. Without retraining, the iSLEEPS-trained model retained respiratory AUCs of 0.833 on ISRUC-I and 0.841 on UCD. These findings support representation-consistent neural adaptation and joint physiological modeling across stroke, healthy-sleep, and sleep-disorder cohorts.

academic.title: The Metrology Atlas: describing recorded physiological data as a measurement system, with VitalDB as a first application
academic.summary: Every value in a recorded physiological dataset is a pair: a recorded time and a recorded value. Neither is the truth. The time comes from a clock that drifts and is corrected in jumps, and often describes a window that ended earlier. The value was quantised, rounded, sometimes heaped by hand, and measured by an instrument with its own error. We present the Metrology Atlas, a dataset-independent way of describing a recorded dataset as a measurement system, and its first application, to VitalDB, an open dataset of 6,388 surgical patients, as a proof of principle. For every variable, the atlas states what was measured, the measurement model linking it to the recorded pair, and what is known about the true time and true value given a record. Each part of the model carries its evidence: 69 studies, 49 parameters and 54 observations, each marked as measured, derived, estimated or assumed. The atlas maps 11 clocks and 14 devices into one timing network, and closes loops in that network to test its own model. Synchronisation reduces the median timing error between the EEG and ECG from 794 ms to 42 ms, and between ventilator and monitor waveforms from 378 ms to 55 ms. The atlas also documents data-quality issues, several of which correct the dataset's own documentation. It is published as a website and a single machine-readable file, with open-source code and a scheme of time-aware labels. Everything is open under CC BY 4.0 and MIT licences. The engine, schema and timing tools carry over unchanged, and the aim is to describe many other datasets the same way.

No formal efficacy or safety endpoints are defined. | Summary: Strados Labs has developed the Strados™ Respiratory Care Platform, including the RESP™ Biosensor System, which encompasses a clinically validated wearable, non-invasive, Bluetooth-enabled device capable of remotely collecting respiratory data. RESP was designed to extend both the geographical and temporal range of lung sound recordings, which can improve the remote monitoring of high-risk COPD patients. The RESP Biosensor continuously captures lung sounds and chest wall motions that are wirelessly transmitted through a mobile app to a web application to be analyzed for changes in respiratory health. Preliminary data suggest good patient compliance and the potential for RESP to detect early COPD exacerbation. However, uncertainty on the optimal RESP monitoring procedure and insufficient longitudinal RESP data for definitive statistical correlation with COPD exacerbations warrant further study. We plan to conduct an observational study to assess feasibility of home RESP remote patient monitoring and secondarily collect the longitudinal data necessary to establish the correlation between RESP based measures and standard of care measures of COPD symptom severity.

scarcityTaxonomy.note: Top Signals selection rubric. Each Top Signals item MUST be labeled with exactly one category from `categories`, assigned a frequency anchor (`annual`/`quarterly`/`monthly`), and scored as `base_score × anchor_weight`. LLM only does category+anchor matching — it does NOT need historical knowledge (categories define scarcity, not LLM memory). Revise quarterly based on dogfooding.

anchor_definitions.annual: Once-a-year or rarer event within this category (e.g., FDA's first consumer-grade AFib clearance for a wearable — happens at most once a year globally).
anchor_definitions.quarterly: Few-per-year event within this category (e.g., a major vendor's new regulatory clearance in a new jurisdiction).
anchor_definitions.monthly: Routine-but-still-notable within this category (e.g., another vendor achieving a similar clearance that's already established).

categories.criteria: FDA 510(k) / De Novo / PMA, CE mark MDR, NMPA certification, PMDA, TGA — for a wearable health feature. Peer-reviewed multi-site prospective clinical validation also qualifies.
examples_positive: Apple Watch gets FDA clearance for new sleep apnea detection
Samsung Health Monitor BP approved in US
Oura ring NMPA class-II certification
examples_negative: Another vendor clones an already-approved feature in a new region (→ monthly anchor, not annual)

categories.criteria: Company or academic publicly releases model weights, pretrained foundation model, large labeled dataset, or production-grade SDK/code for wearable/physiological signals. Must be usable (not just a paper claiming 'code coming soon').
examples_positive: Meta releases wearable foundation model weights on HuggingFace
Stanford/Apple release 1M-ECG labeled dataset
Google open-sources Fitbit sleep staging model
examples_negative: Academic paper promises code release but repo is empty

categories.criteria: M&A, major exec/founder departure or appointment at a wearable company, large funding round (≥$50M), strategic pivot announcement. Affects competitive landscape or talent flow.
examples_positive: Google acquires Oura
Shwetak Patel leaves Google Health for X startup
WHOOP pivots from consumer to B2B-clinical

categories.criteria: Consumer wearable first-time integration of a physical/biochemical sensing modality (non-invasive BP, non-invasive glucose, EMG, sweat cortisol, SpHb, real-time hydration, etc.). Must ship in a real product, not just a research paper.
examples_positive: Samsung ships first consumer non-invasive glucose on Galaxy Watch
Apple adds wrist-based cuffless BP to Series X
Oura integrates continuous sweat-lactate sensor
examples_negative: New optical HR sensor iteration in existing form factor (already-done modality)
Academic prototype for a new sensor — belongs in algorithmic_breakthrough or open_release if qualifying

categories.criteria: New SOTA with concrete metric on wearable/physiological task, OR foundation-model / self-supervised training at ≥10M-sample scale, OR on-device breakthrough with specific latency/size/power numbers. Must have reproducible evidence (paper with code, benchmark result).
examples_positive: ECG foundation model at 11M samples with systematic SSL comparison (example)
On-device AFib detection at <5ms/inference on Apple S10 chip
New sleep-stage SOTA on SHHS with 3pp gain
examples_negative: Incremental +1pp gain with cherry-picked test set

categories.criteria: Prospective or multi-site clinical study with n≥10,000 participants OR multi-center design, wearable-derived endpoint, peer-reviewed or at top conference.
examples_positive: Ultrahuman Ring N=3086 longitudinal sleep study (today's example — note: n<10k but near-threshold + longitudinal design keeps it in this category at monthly anchor)
All of Us cohort wearable analysis n>50k
Apple Heart Study n=419k

categories.criteria: Wearable vendor first-time entry into new go-to-market category: clinical services, B2B/B2B2C, insurance, subscription, EHR integration, pharma partnership. Must be a real product launch, not a trial balloon.
examples_positive: WHOOP launches clinician video visits + HealthEx EHR integration (today's example)
Oura partners with large insurer for reimbursed rings
Apple Watch Atrial Fibrillation History gets CMS reimbursement code
examples_negative: New subscription tier of existing product

categories.criteria: HealthKit / Health Connect / Samsung Health SDK / Huawei Health Kit / Wear OS schema, new data type, permission, or interoperability standard (FHIR wearables profile). Must be shipping, not WWDC keynote hype.
examples_positive: HealthKit adds glucose trend data type in watchOS 27
Health Connect adds cross-app mental-health schema
New IEEE standard for wearable data exchange ratified
